title: Long noncoding RNA Malat1 protects against osteoporosis and bone metastasis

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section describing Fig. 2, immediately after the femoral TRAP-staining paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text is materially out of order and duplicates a paragraph. It first ends mid-sentence: "TRAP staining revealed a significant increase in osteoclasts in the femurs of Malat1−/− mice compared with Malat1+/+" and then starts the LPS-calvarial experiment. After an ellipsis, it resumes the unfinished sentence with "mice, and this increase was reversed..." and repeats the entire LPS-calvarial paragraph beginning "Next, to determine the role of Malat1 in modulating pathological bone loss...". This produces two copies of the same experiment and interrupts the preceding result, requiring correction of the Results/Fig. 2 narrative.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract; Results section "Untreated osteoporosis is associated..." through Fig. 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly presents direct intratibial tumor implantation as evidence that host Malat1 protects against "bone metastasis." B16F1 or EO771 cells were "injected ... into the tibiae," which bypasses tumor-cell escape from a primary tumor, circulation, homing, extravasation, and initial bone colonization. Such experiments assess growth/survival of already implanted tumor cells in bone (an intraosseous tumor-growth model), not metastatic dissemination or metastatic propensity. The later wording "metastatic bone colonization" remains inaccurate for direct intratibial implantation. The results can support altered local tumor burden/osteolysis after intraosseous injection, but not the stated conclusion that Malat1 prevents bone metastasis.

predicted_errors.error_location: Clinical single-cell RNA-seq analysis, Fig. 4 description
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed between-condition clinical comparison has no replicated non-osteoporotic reference group. The stated GSE169396 material contains "bone tissues from a non-osteoporotic individual and three osteoporosis patients," yet the authors claim that expression in osteoporosis, osteosarcoma, and breast-cancer-metastasis patients was "significantly lower ... than in the non-osteoporotic individual." A single control donor cannot establish a control distribution or support a patient-group statistical comparison. Moreover, the normal control and each disease group come from different datasets/studies; disease status is therefore confounded with study/batch. Harmony alignment does not create biological control replicates or remove donor/study confounding. Cell-level testing without donor-level pseudobulk or adequately replicated matched controls would pseudoreplicate cells and cannot support the asserted clinical association.
